planting.note: Set divisions or plugs in spring into saturated to shallowly flooded, acidic soil in the dappled shade of a bottomland planting; mulch with leaf litter to mimic the swamp-floor conditions it needs.

directions: Greater marsh St. John's-wort is the shade-tolerant member of its genus, growing naturally in the standing water and deep leaf litter of bottomland hardwood swamps and cypress-tupelo flats across the lower Mississippi Alluvial Valley and southeastern coastal plain, where it persists in far less light than its sun-loving relatives. Slender upright stems carry pairs of blue-green leaves and open small salmon-pink, five-petaled flowers for a few hours on summer afternoons, a subtle but welcome bloom in deep swamp shade. It is best suited to the saturated, shaded margins of a woodland rain garden or constructed bog rather than a typical sunny perennial bed, and spreads slowly by rhizome to form loose colonies without becoming aggressive. Divide clumps only occasionally, as it resents disturbance and reestablishes slowly after transplanting.

planting.note: Set divisions in spring directly onto a partially submerged rotting log, stump, or hummock in standing water, or into a saturated shaded pond margin; this sedge naturally roots into decaying wood rather than ordinary garden soil.

directions: Log sedge is one of the most distinctive sedges of bottomland hardwood swamps, growing almost exclusively as a tussock perched on half-submerged rotting logs, cypress knees, and stumps within permanently flooded swamp forest across scattered sites in the Mississippi Alluvial Valley and eastern United States. Its arching, grass-like foliage and inconspicuous brownish seedheads make it more a curiosity for the water-garden enthusiast than a showy border plant, best displayed by anchoring a division onto a partly sunken log in a shaded pond or bog feature. Because natural populations are uncommon and considered vulnerable in much of its range, cultivated divisions from a specialty native nursery are strongly preferable to any wild-collected material. Once established on its woody perch it needs little attention beyond keeping the water level from dropping below the log's surface.
